questions.prompt: Why can't most LLM outputs be tested with an exact string match?
options: The same correct answer can be phrased in many ways, and outputs can vary between runs
questions.explanation: Generation is often non-deterministic and many phrasings are correct, so evaluation uses criteria, rubrics and properties instead.

questions.prompt: What is an evaluation set (eval set)?
options: A fixed collection of inputs with expected properties or reference answers, used to score a model or prompt repeatedly
questions.explanation: A stable eval set lets you compare versions on the same cases over time.

questions.prompt: When using a model as a grader (LLM-as-judge), you should check its grades against a sample of human judgements.
questions.explanation: Model graders have biases (length, position, self-preference). Calibrating against human labels shows whether you can trust them.

questions.prompt: Which can be graded reliably with plain code? Select all that apply.
options: The output is valid JSON with the required keys
The answer contains the correct order number
questions.explanation: Structure, length and exact facts are code-checkable. Tone needs human or model judgement with a rubric.

questions.prompt: A prompt change raises your eval score from 82% to 84% on 50 cases. What should you do before declaring it better?
options: Look at which cases changed and consider the noise: one case is 2%; rerun or enlarge the set
questions.explanation: One case flipping explains the difference. Inspect changed cases and use enough examples (and repeated runs) to separate signal from noise.

questions.prompt: Which practice reduces position bias in pairwise LLM-as-judge comparisons?
options: Run each comparison twice with the answer order swapped and only count consistent verdicts
Always put the new answer first
questions.explanation: Judges often prefer the first (or second) option. Swapping order and checking agreement controls for that.

questions.prompt: Your eval set was built from 200 real support tickets last year. A new product line now makes up 30% of tickets, and production complaints rise while eval scores stay at 90%. What is wrong?
options: The eval set no longer represents production; add new, real cases (especially failures) and keep refreshing it
The model is fine because the score is 90%
questions.explanation: Eval sets drift out of date. A score is only meaningful for the distribution it measures.

questions.prompt: A model grader scores answers 1-10 and every answer gets 7-9. What change makes the grading more useful?
options: Use a specific rubric with discrete, observable criteria (e.g. pass/fail per criterion) and examples of each grade
Ask the grader to be more generous
questions.explanation: Vague numeric scales compress into the middle. Concrete binary criteria are more consistent and easier to validate against humans.

coding.title: Code-graded checks for a reply
coding.prompt:
Write `grade(reply, order_id, max_words)` that returns a dict of check -> bool:

- `'mentions_order'`: the order id appears in the reply
- `'length_ok'`: word count (split on whitespace) is at most `max_words`
- `'no_placeholder'`: the reply contains none of `[NAME]`, `{{`, `TODO` (case-sensitive)
- `'polite_close'`: the reply's last non-empty line starts with `Thanks` or `Best` 

Example: `grade('Hi,\nOrder A-17 ships today.\nThanks, Support', 'A-17', 50)` returns all True.
coding.explanation: Deterministic checks are cheap, fast and never flaky, so use them for every property that code can decide and save human or model judgement for the rest.
hints: `str.split()` with no argument splits on any whitespace.
Ignore empty lines when finding the last line.

tests.name: All pass
tests.code:
r = grade('Hi,\nOrder A-17 ships today.\nThanks, Support', 'A-17', 50)
assert r == {'mentions_order': True, 'length_ok': True, 'no_placeholder': True, 'polite_close': True}, r

tests.name: Detects failures
tests.code:
r = grade('Dear [NAME], your order ships.\n\n', 'A-17', 3)
assert r == {'mentions_order': False, 'length_ok': False, 'no_placeholder': False, 'polite_close': False}, r

coding.title: Grader agreement with humans
coding.prompt:
Write `agreement(human, model)` for two equal-length lists of binary labels (1 = pass, 0 = fail). Return a dict with `'accuracy'` (fraction of matches) and `'kappa'` (Cohen's kappa), both rounded to 3 decimals. Kappa = (po - pe) / (1 - pe) where po is accuracy and pe = p_h1*p_m1 + p_h0*p_m0 (the marginal proportions). If `pe == 1`, return kappa 1.0.

Example: `agreement([1,1,0,0], [1,0,0,0])` returns `{'accuracy': 0.75, 'kappa': 0.5}`.
coding.solution:
def agreement(human, model):
    n = len(human)
    po = sum(h == m for h, m in zip(human, model)) / n
    ph1 = sum(human) / n
    pm1 = sum(model) / n
    pe = ph1 * pm1 + (1 - ph1) * (1 - pm1)
    kappa = 1.0 if pe == 1 else (po - pe) / (1 - pe)
    return {'accuracy': round(po, 3), 'kappa': round(kappa, 3)}
coding.explanation: Raw accuracy looks high when most answers pass, because a grader that always says pass agrees often by chance. Kappa subtracts chance agreement, so it tells you whether the model grader is really tracking human judgement.
hints: pe uses each rater's own proportion of 1s.
Guard the pe == 1 case to avoid division by zero.
